title: Floor, Ceiling & Counting
goal: Compute floors, ceilings and absolute values without sign slips, and count multiples in any interval, including "divisible by `a` or `b`" questions.
magic: Floor = step left to an integer; ceiling = step right. `⌊−2.7⌋ = −3`.
`|x|` = distance from 0; evaluate the inside first.
AND → `lcm`. OR → add both, subtract the AND.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
Floor rounds down, ceiling rounds up (on the number line)
blocks.summary: `⌊x⌋` is the nearest integer at or below `x`; `⌈x⌉` the nearest at or above. "Down" means towards −∞, even for negatives.
blocks.picture: You're in a building on floor 2.7 (between floors). The floor under your feet is floor 2; the ceiling above you is floor 3. In a basement at −2.7, the floor under you is −3, not −2.
blocks.official: `⌊·⌋ : ℝ → ℤ`, the **floor** of `x`: the greatest integer `≤ x`. `⌈·⌉ : ℝ → ℤ`, the **ceiling**: the least integer `≥ x` (Week 1, slide 10). Example: `⌊π⌋ = 3 = ⌈e⌉`. For an integer `n`, `⌊n⌋ = ⌈n⌉ = n`.

steps: `−2.7` sits between −3 and −2 on the number line (−3 is further left).
watch.answer: **2, 3, −3, −2.** For negatives, floor moves away from 0.

tries.why: `√10 ≈ 3.16`, and the next integer up is 4.
An integer is its own floor and ceiling.

trap.test: Draw the number line. Floor = the integer to the **left**.

blocks.magic: Floor = step left to an integer. Ceiling = step right. Integers stay put.

blocks.title: Two rules: negatives flip, integers slide out
blocks.summary: `⌊−x⌋ = −⌈x⌉`, and adding an integer `t` inside just adds `t` outside.
blocks.picture: A mirror: reflect `x` to `−x`, and "down" becomes "up". And sliding everything along by whole floors doesn't change which floor you're above.
blocks.official: Simple properties (Week 1, slide 11): `⌊−x⌋ = −⌈x⌉`, hence `⌈x⌉ = −⌊−x⌋`. `⌊x + t⌋ = ⌊x⌋ + t` and `⌈x + t⌉ = ⌈x⌉ + t` **for all `t ∈ ℤ`**.

watch.q: Use the rules to find `⌊−4.3⌋` and `⌊6.25 + 10⌋`.

tries.a: **No** (the left is an integer, the right isn't). The rule needs `t ∈ ℤ`.

trap.correct: The negation turns floor into **ceiling**: `⌊−x⌋ = −⌈x⌉`. (`⌊−1.5⌋ = −2`, but `−⌊1.5⌋ = −1`.)

blocks.magic: `⌊−x⌋ = −⌈x⌉`. `⌊x + t⌋ = ⌊x⌋ + t` only when `t` is an integer.

blocks.title: Absolute value: distance from 0
blocks.picture: How far is a floor from ground level? Floor 4 and basement −4 are both 4 floors away.
blocks.official: `|x| = x` if `x ≥ 0`, and `|x| = −x` if `x < 0` (Week 1, slide 16). So `|x| ≥ 0` always, and `|x| = |−x|`. Order matters when you mix it with floor/ceiling: do the innermost operation first.

watch.answer: **2** vs **3**: the order of operations changes the answer.

tries.why: Compute inside first: `−5`, then drop the sign.
By the definition, `|x| = −x` when `x < 0`, and at `x = 0` both sides are 0.

trap.tempting: `|x|` just deletes a minus sign you can see.
trap.correct: `|x|` is `−x` whenever `x < 0`, even if `x` is written without a minus (e.g. `x = a − b` with `a < b`).
trap.test: Evaluate the inside to a number first, then apply the definition.

blocks.magic: `|x|` = distance from 0. Evaluate the inside first.

blocks.title: Floors of sums: `⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋` can be 1 less than `⌊x + y⌋`
blocks.summary: The fractional parts can add up to more than 1, which adds an extra whole number.
blocks.picture: Two jars each 0.6 full don't count as a full jar each, but pour them together and you get 1 full jar (plus a bit).
blocks.official: Lecture exercise 1.1.19(a) (Week 1, slides 12–13): find `x, y` with `⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ < ⌊x + y⌋`; answer `⌊3π⌋ + ⌊e⌋ = 9 + 2 = 11 < 12 = ⌊3π + e⌋`. In general `⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋ ≤ ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ + 1`. Related: `⌈x⌉ − ⌊x⌋` is 0 if `x` is an integer, and 1 otherwise.

watch.answer: **0 < 1**: the two fractions combine into an extra whole.

tries.why: Works whenever the fractional parts add to less than 1.
`⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋` is an integer `≤ x + y`, and `⌊x + y⌋` is the **greatest** such integer.

check.expr: all(floor(a/10) + floor(b/10) <= floor(a/10 + b/10) for a in range(-50, 50) for b in range(-50, 50))

trap.correct: Only sometimes. It fails when the fractional parts add up to 1 or more.

blocks.title: Counting multiples of `k` in `[n, m]`
blocks.summary: Multiples of `k` up to `m`, minus those up to `n − 1`: `⌊m/k⌋ − ⌊(n − 1)/k⌋`.
blocks.picture: How many buses leave every 15 minutes between minute 20 and minute 100? Count those up to 100, subtract those that already left before minute 20.
blocks.official: **Fact** (Week 1, slide 11): for `k > 0` and `m ≥ n`, the number of multiples of `k` in the interval `[n, m]` is `⌊m/k⌋ − ⌊(n − 1)/k⌋`. It works for negative `n` too, as long as you take the floor correctly.

watch.q: How many multiples of 4 are in `[10, 50]`?

tries.q: How many multiples of 5 are in `[1, 99]`?
How many multiples of 3 are in `[−10, 10]`?
How many multiples of 9 are in `[−50, −1]`?
How many multiples of 5 are in `[2026, 2100]`?

trap.correct: That throws away `n` itself when `n` is a multiple. Subtract the multiples **strictly below** `n`: `⌊(n − 1)/k⌋`.
trap.test: Test on a tiny case: multiples of 5 in `[5, 5]` should be 1.

blocks.title: Divisible by `a` AND `b`, or by `a` OR `b`
blocks.summary: "By `a` and `b`" = by `lcm(a, b)`. "By `a` or `b`" = count(a) + count(b) − count(both).
blocks.picture: At a party, 20 people like pizza and 15 like sushi. If 5 like both, only 30 people like at least one: the 5 were counted twice.
blocks.official: A number is divisible by both `a` and `b` exactly when it is divisible by `lcm(a, b)` (Week 1, slide 15). To count "`a` or `b`", add the two counts and subtract the double-counted ones: `|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|` (Week 1, slide 33).

watch.q: How many numbers in `[100, 999]` are divisible by 4 or by 6?

tries.q: Same interval `[100, 999]`: how many are divisible by **neither** 4 nor 6?
tries.why: The interval has `999 − 100 + 1 = 900` numbers; subtract the 300 divisible by 4 or 6.

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(100, 1000) if x % 4 and x % 6)

tries.q: Same interval: divisible by 6 but **not** by 4?
tries.why: By 6: 150. Remove those also divisible by 4 (that's by 12): `150 − 75`.

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(100, 1000) if x % 6 == 0 and x % 4)

tries.q: How many in `[1, 500]` are divisible by 7 or 11?

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(1, 501) if x % 7 == 0 or x % 11 == 0)

trap.correct: Use `lcm(4, 6) = 12`. 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6, but not by 24.
trap.test: The product works only when the numbers are coprime (e.g. 7 and 11).

blocks.magic: AND → `lcm`. OR → add both, subtract the AND.

items.why: Down means left on the number line.

blocks.sub: Problem set 1, Q1(a) and Q2(b) style: floor/ceiling one-liners and counting multiples in an interval. Original numbers.

items.q: How many numbers in `[3000, 9000]` are divisible by (a) 4, (b) 10, (c) 4 and 10, (d) 4 or 10?
items.wrong: If you used 40 for (c): `4 × 10 = 40` misses 20, 60, 100, … Use the lcm.

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(3000, 9001) if x % 4 == 0 or x % 10 == 0)

items.q: How many numbers in `[150, 1500]` are divisible by 6 or 9?

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(150, 1501) if x % 6 == 0 or x % 9 == 0)

items.q: How many numbers in `[−100, 100]` are divisible by 3 or 4?

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(-100, 101) if x % 3 == 0 or x % 4 == 0)

items.q: Use the slide-11 formula to count the even integers in `[−7, 12]`.
How many numbers in `[1, 1000]` are divisible by 2, 3 or 5?
items.why: Inclusion–exclusion for three: `500 + 333 + 200 − (166 + 100 + 66) + 33 = 734` (pairs use lcm 6, 10, 15; the triple uses 30).

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(1, 1001) if x % 2 == 0 or x % 3 == 0 or x % 5 == 0)

items.q: How many perfect squares `≤ 10 000` end in the digit 1? (No calculator.)
items.why: `n² ≤ 10 000` means `n ≤ 100`. `n²` ends in 1 exactly when `n` ends in 1 or 9. That's 1, 9, 11, 19, …, 91, 99: 10 decades × 2.

check.expr: sum(1 for n in range(1, 101) if (n*n) % 10 == 1)

items.q: The lecture's supplementary exercise 1.8.9 ends with "try the same question for `n⁴`": how many fourth powers `≤ 1 000 000` end in 9?
items.why: Last digits of `n⁴` can only be 0, 1, 5 or 6 (check `n = 0 … 9`). None ends in 9.

check.expr: sum(1 for n in range(1, 101) if isqrt(n) == 7)

items.a: **Exactly when the fractional part of `x` is less than ½.**
items.why: Write `x = n + f` with `n = ⌊x⌋`, `0 ≤ f < 1`. Then `⌊2x⌋ = 2n + ⌊2f⌋`, and `⌊2f⌋ = 0` iff `f < ½`.

check.expr: all((floor(2*(k/8)) == 2*floor(k/8)) == ((k/8 - floor(k/8)) < 0.5) for k in range(-40, 41))

items.q: Formula for the number of multiples of `k` in `[n, m]`?

check.expr: sum(1 for x in range(1, 61) if x % 4 == 0 or x % 6 == 0)

lines: `⌊x⌋`: greatest integer `≤ x`. `⌈x⌉`: least integer `≥ x`. Negatives: floor moves away from 0.
Count multiples: `⌊m/k⌋ − ⌊(n − 1)/k⌋`. Both → lcm. Either → `A + B − both`.
